conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The gallbladder fluid grew E. coli. We’re waiting on sensitivity results to confirm the best antibiotic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The E. coli is resistant to several antibiotics, including piperacillin-tazobactam. It’s only intermediate to meropenem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Intermediate? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means meropenem might not be strong enough. We’re switching to tigecycline, which the bacteria are sensitive to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve checked. It’s safe. You’ll get it IV every 12 hours for 7 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re placing a PICC line today so you can finish antibiotics at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: At home? I’m getting better that fast?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your vitals are stable, you’re afebrile, and labs are improving. The PICC will let you get IV antibiotics safely at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chest X-ray after PICC placement showed the tip was too deep—down in the right atrium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can cause irritation. They repositioned it. The next X-ray shows it’s now in the mid superior vena cava—perfect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count is down to 4.8. That’s normal. You’re fighting the infection well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the drain? When does that come out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. You’ll need it for a few months. Interventional radiology will replace it in about three months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the bile duct drain? I noticed it’s capped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The imaging shows it’s coiled back on itself but still working. No blockage. We’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue tigecycline via PICC for 7 days. Keep taking oral vancomycin for C. diff prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain? I’ve been on oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue your pain meds as needed. Also keep using stool softeners—your bowels have been slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any signs I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fever, increased abdominal pain, redness or drainage at the PICC or drain sites. Call us if any of those happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. All your labs are stable. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Will I see you again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have a phone follow-up in two weeks. Also see interventional radiology in three months for the drain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my cancer treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished cycle 8. Your oncologist will discuss next steps after you’ve recovered from this infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate everything you’ve done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot. Focus on resting and finishing your antibiotics. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—what about the constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using polyethylene glycol and senna. Drink plenty of fluids. Let your primary doctor know if it doesn’t improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure and prostate meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue both—atenolol and terazosin—as before. No changes needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the rosacea cream?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep using metronidazole cream as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the DNR status—is that still in place?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your DNR status remains. It’s documented in your chart and will be respected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have the discharge papers ready soon. A nurse will go over all the instructions with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to follow up with everyone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best thing you can do. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. You're here because of abdominal pain and fevers. We’re concerned this might be another episode of cholangitis, especially given your history of cholangiocarcinoma and biliary stents.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain in my right side has been getting worse, and I’ve had chills all night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your CT scan from earlier today. It shows your biliary stents are still in place, but the bile ducts on the right side look more dilated than before, which suggests a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be why I’m so sick again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The blockage can cause bile to back up and get infected—this is cholangitis. We’ve started broad-spectrum antibiotics because you’ve had resistant bacteria before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time—it was E. coli, right? And it didn’t respond well to regular antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s correct. So we’re starting you on a combination that covers resistant organisms. We’ll narrow it down once we get blood culture results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about the drain I have? It’s been draining green fluid like usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s your biliary drain, and the green bile is normal. We’ll keep monitoring the output. We also need to check if your gallbladder drain is working properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been feeling nauseous and vomited once last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added ondansetron for nausea. That should help. We’ll keep an eye on your labs too—your liver enzymes and bilirubin are elevated, which fits with bile duct obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be here this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It depends on how quickly you respond to antibiotics and whether we need a procedure. We’re planning an ERCP to look at the blockage and possibly clear it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. It’s not too bad. When would it happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled it for tomorrow morning. In the meantime, we’ll keep you on IV fluids and antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. We’re getting ready for your ERCP. The goal is to open up the blocked bile duct and make sure your stents are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they put in a new stent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The radiology team will decide based on what they see. You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ERCP went well. They found your stent was partially blocked, and they cleared it. No new stent was needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. Do you think that’ll help with the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, relieving the blockage is key. Now the bile can drain properly, which should help the antibiotics work better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My pain is already a little better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll keep monitoring your temperature and repeat blood work to see how you’re responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound yesterday to check the bile ducts. The right side doesn’t look more dilated, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the spleen? I remember they said it was big.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s mildly enlarged, but that’s been stable. It’s not a concern right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My stomach’s been a little off—any chance it’s C. diff again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested your stool, and it was positive. So we’re starting you on oral vancomycin to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, I remember that helped last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures have come back negative for growth so far. That’s a good sign—no bacteria in the blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotics are working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks that way. We’re going to place a PICC line today so you can finish IV antibiotics at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that be uncomfortable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a quick procedure with local anesthesia. You’ll have it in your arm and it’ll allow a nurse to give your antibiotics at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line is in and working well. Chest X-ray confirms it’s positioned correctly in the superior vena cava.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’d like to get home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re on track for discharge in a few days. We need to make sure your infection is fully controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your blood cultures are negative now—no growth after 48 hours. That means the bacteremia has cleared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your liver function tests are also improving—bilirubin is down to 0.5 and enzymes are normalizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the antibiotics? How long do I need them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll finish a 14-day course from the time your blood cultures turned negative. That means about two more weeks of IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vancomycin for C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll finish that too—another week should do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. A visiting nurse will come to your home to give the IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need to take care of my drains, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Empty the drainage bag daily and record the amount. Change the dressing every three days using sterile water or half-strength hydrogen peroxide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I flush the drain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, do not flush it. If the flow slows or the site becomes painful or red, call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my pain meds—I’ll keep taking them as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue your regular pain medications. We’ve added mirtazapine at night to help with appetite and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I’ve been a little down lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning are stable. White count is still low but improving. We’re comfortable discharging you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to come back for follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with your oncologist and the interventional radiology team to manage your drains. We’ll send the details to your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the DNR status—I want to make sure that’s still in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your DNR status is documented and will be communicated to all providers involved in your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. You’re cleared to go home. The nurse will review your medications and drain care one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve responded well. Keep taking the IV antibiotics as scheduled, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to write down the drain output every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, Mr. Johnson. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening, Mr. Johnson. I’m Dr. Patel, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in with a fever and some concerns about your drain. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I had chills and a low-grade fever at home, and I noticed my gallbladder drain wasn’t draining like it should—only about 30 cc instead of my usual 60 or 70. And the dressing was soaked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned you felt pressure in your right upper abdomen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a dull pressure. It feels similar to when I’ve had blockages before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. We’ve reviewed your records. You’ve had a complex history with cholangiocarcinoma, biliary stents, and infections. We’re concerned your gallbladder drain may have shifted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think it might have caught on a cabinet a few days ago. I didn’t think much of it at the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could explain it. We’re going to do a CT scan of your abdomen to check the position of the drain and see if there’s any infection or blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve been through this before, but it’s always scary when the fever comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re here to help. We’ve started you on antibiotics—meropenem and tigecycline—to cover possible infections until we get more information.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on tigecycline recently. I stopped a few days ago—was that too soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on your last discharge, you were supposed to continue for 14 days after the last positive culture. If you stopped early, that might have contributed to the recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize. I thought I was done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. We’ll make sure you complete the right course this time. Let’s focus on getting the CT done first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, your CT scan is back. The gallbladder drain has partially come out and is now coiled in your abdominal wall. Your gallbladder is dilated and inflamed—this is causing your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not working anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The radiology team will replace it today under ultrasound guidance. That should relieve the pressure and help treat the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it be painful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get some sedation and local anesthesia. Most patients tolerate it well. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Mr. Johnson. The procedure went well. The new drain is properly placed in your gallbladder, and we’ve sent fluid for testing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I already feel a bit better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. The lab results show Pseudomonas and a resistant strain of E. coli in the bile. That explains why you got sick again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are those dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They can be, but we’re treating them appropriately. We’ll continue tigecycline for your resistant E. coli and add ciprofloxacin to cover the Pseudomonas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken cipro before. Is it safe with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve checked. It’s safe. You’ll take it by mouth twice a day for 14 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the IV tigecycline?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue that twice daily for 14 days total. We’ll place a midline for easier access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I go home with the IV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but only for a few more days. Since it’s less than 14 days total, you won’t need formal home health nursing—just a caregiver to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My wife can help. What about the vancomycin I’m on for C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked a stool test—it’s negative for C. diff. But because you’ve had severe episodes before, we’ll keep the vancomycin until you finish the other antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll keep taking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your fever is gone, and your labs are improving. White count is down, and liver enzymes are trending better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. I feel much better today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The infectious disease team agrees. We’ll keep you on the same antibiotics. Your drain is working well—drainage is clear and decreasing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need this drain long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The radiology team will contact you about follow-up. For now, it’s essential for preventing another infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Mr. Johnson. Your latest labs show continued improvement. Platelets are stable, and your bilirubin is down to 0.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. We’ll make sure your midline is secure and that your wife knows how to manage the IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my cancer? Should I see my oncologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your last chemo was recent. Your oncologists recommend holding off for a few months due to these infections. We’ve also introduced you to palliative care for support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. I want to stay comfortable and make good decisions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll support you in that. You mentioned you want full code status—that’s documented.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your labs are excellent. You’re afebrile, eating well, and your drain output is minimal. We’re planning discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue ciprofloxacin twice daily and tigecycline IV twice daily for 14 days total. Finish the vancomycin when those are done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the drain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep the dressing clean and dry. Radiology will call you for follow-up. Call us if you see redness, increased pain, or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, doctor. I feel lucky to have such a good team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad you’re on the mend. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, just confirming—you’re discharged now. Medications are ready, and your wife has the IV instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, everything’s set. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Remember to restart your atenolol for blood pressure and migraines. And call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I've reviewed your case. You came in with severe abdominal pain and vomiting last night. We’ve run some tests, and it looks like your biliary drain might be blocked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain was terrible. And I saw blood in my drain bag at home. That scared me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That’s called hemobilia—bleeding into the bile ducts. We’re concerned the stent or drain might be irritated or blocked, which can cause both pain and bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that damage my liver? My enzymes were high last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly why we’re acting fast. Your liver enzymes—ALT and AST—are elevated, which suggests stress on the liver due to bile backing up. We need to clear the blockage to protect your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Interventional radiology is already on it. They’ll replace your biliary drain with a larger one and clean out the stents. This should restore bile flow and relieve the pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe? I’ve had complications before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a standard procedure for patients like you. They’ll use imaging to guide it precisely. There’s a small risk of bleeding, which we’re monitoring closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. They exchanged your drain and cleared the stent. Bile is now flowing freely. Your pain should start improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already feel a bit better. But I passed bright red blood in my stool earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s concerning. It could be related to the bleeding in your bile duct. We’ve called GI. They recommend an ERCP tomorrow to look inside and see where the bleeding is coming from.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: ERCP? I’ve had that before. Is it painful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel it. It’s important to find and stop the bleeding. We’ll monitor you closely after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ERCP showed blood coming from your right hepatic stent. There was sludge and some active bleeding. We cleared the sludge, but the source of bleeding needs further evaluation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not fixed yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not completely. The bleeding likely comes from a small artery near the drain. Interventional radiology will do an angiogram to find and block that vessel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another procedure? How risky is that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s minimally invasive. They’ll go through a small puncture in your groin to reach the artery. The goal is to stop the bleeding without surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did the angiogram. We found an abnormal artery near your biliary drain, likely feeding into the bleeding site. We couldn’t block it yesterday, but we’ll try again tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s still bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We haven’t seen active bleeding since the ERCP, but the source is still there. The second procedure should seal it off. You’ll be moved to the ICU tonight for closer monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news. The embolization was successful. They blocked the artery feeding the bleed. Your drain is clear, and your labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the fever I had last night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a low-grade fever, so we started antibiotics—vancomycin and meropenem—just in case. Your blood cultures came back negative, so it’s likely not a serious infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m on antibiotics now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for now. Infectious disease reviewed your case. Given your history of resistant infections, they want to continue the IV antibiotics for a few more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your platelet count dropped a bit. We’re watching it closely. It’s likely due to your illness and the antibiotics, not something more serious like HIT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. It’s mild and improving. We’ll keep monitoring. No treatment needed unless it drops further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows some fluid around the lungs. It’s not pneumonia, but we’ll do a CT to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it cancer spreading?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT will help us know for sure. But given your history, we suspect it’s fluid buildup from inflammation, not new cancer. We’ll know more tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT shows moderate pleural effusions—fluid around the lungs—but no signs of infection or cancer spread. It’s likely related to your recent procedures and inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with time and treatment. We’ll monitor it. If it causes breathing issues, we can drain it, but for now, it’s stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are much better. Liver enzymes are down, white count is improving, and your bile culture showed mixed bacteria, but no C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. We’ll stop the IV antibiotics since there’s no active infection. But you’ll continue oral vancomycin to prevent C. diff, as per infectious disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. How long do I take it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Until the 10th. It’s just a precaution because of your antibiotic exposure and history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your drain is now capped. We’ll make sure it stays clear. You’ll follow up with interventional radiology in a week for routine maintenance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my cancer? Should I see my oncologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have an appointment scheduled with Dr. Lee next week. There’s no sign of progression on recent scans, so your current plan remains stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, you’re doing well. We’re discharging you today. Your bleeding is controlled, liver function is improving, and you’re no longer febrile.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you have fever, abdominal pain, or notice blood in your stool or drain. Keep your follow-up appointments with radiology and oncology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it three times a day until the 10th. It’s just to protect your gut while your system recovers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. Any nausea or pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your drain site looks clean. Remember to keep it dry and covered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your meds and instructions one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I've been reviewing why you came in today. You had dizziness and then fevers, and your biliary drain wasn’t draining. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. I was at my urologist yesterday, felt dizzy, then got chills overnight. This morning, no bile was coming out of the drain. And I vomited a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The outside hospital checked your labs and saw your bilirubin was going up, so they sent you here. We’ve already done a procedure today to clean and replace your biliary drain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, already? I didn’t know that happened. How did it go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The interventional radiology team did a balloon sweep to open up the blockage and replaced the catheter. There’s better flow now, but we think there might be other blockages higher up in your stents.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I got so sick? Because the bile couldn’t get out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. When bile backs up, it can cause infection—called cholangitis. You had fevers and a fast heart rate, which are signs of early sepsis. We’ve started you on antibiotics called Unasyn.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sepsis? That sounds serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is, but we caught it early. We’re treating it aggressively. We also drew blood cultures to see if there’s a bloodstream infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to do an MRCP tomorrow—a special MRI of your bile ducts—to see if there are other blockages. And we’ll keep monitoring your labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. Your blood culture from last night just came back positive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Positive? So I do have an infection in my blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s E. coli, a type of bacteria that can live in the gut but causes trouble when it gets into the bile or blood. Because of your history, we’re switching your antibiotic to meropenem, which works better against this strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that stronger? Any more side effects?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s more targeted. It’s generally well tolerated. We’ll give it every six hours through your IV. The infectious disease team agrees this is the best choice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. What about the MRCP?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s scheduled for later today. It’ll help us see if your metal stents are blocked and where. That’ll guide the next step—possibly another ERCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I have the MRCP results. There’s mild dilation in the left bile ducts with some narrowing. The stents are in place, and there’s air in the ducts, which means they’re open. But there’s also signs of inflammation—cholangitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the stents are open but still inflamed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The infection is likely coming from debris or sludge in the stents. We’ve scheduled an ERCP for tomorrow to clean them out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another ERCP? I’ve had a few of those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s not fun, but it’s the best way to clear the blockage. The team will remove any stones or sludge. After that, we’ll cap your biliary drain if things look good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your ERCP went well. They removed sludge and debris from both stents. The flow looks much better. We’re going to cap your drain and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I won’t need the drain bag anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. We’ll monitor you. If you develop fever, pain, or nausea, we’ll reopen it. But the goal is to keep it capped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’d be a relief. My blood sugar’s been high too—did you see that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your glucose was 252. We’re calling that newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes. We’ll manage it with diet, a diabetic meal plan, and sliding scale insulin for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was afraid of that. My dad had diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help you manage it. Also, we held your atenolol for migraines because of the infection—we didn’t want your blood pressure too low. We’ll restart it when you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. Liver enzymes are coming down—bilirubin is now 0.6, which is great. Your white count was low yesterday but is stable today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel better—no fever, no nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re tolerating regular food, and your drain is still capped. We’ll keep you on meropenem for a full 10-day course, which means you’ll go home on IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: At home? How will I get the IV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A home health nurse will come to give it every six hours. We’ll set that up. You’ll also take oral vancomycin to prevent C. diff, since you’ve had it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had it three times—don’t want it again. So vancomycin until the IV ends?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Then stop both on the same day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge planning. We’re aiming for Friday. You’ll follow up with your oncologist and PCP for liver tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I get sick again before then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop fever, pain, nausea, or vomiting, uncuff your biliary drain and call the GI fellow. That lets bile drain out and can prevent another infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my cancer—does this affect my treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This episode is about the infection and blockage. Your oncologist will continue your cholangiocarcinoma care as planned. This doesn’t change that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge. Your vitals are stable—temperature normal, heart rate 74. You’re walking, eating, and feeling well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I really feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your exam shows soft belly, no tenderness. The upper drain is capped, lower one to bag. We’ll send you home with the IV setup and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll see my PCP next week for liver tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your oncologist as scheduled. We’ll also arrange home health for the IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did well. Just watch for any return of symptoms and follow the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, your discharge orders are ready. You’re cleared to go home with services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m ready to get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Here’s your discharge summary. Remember: if you get fevers or pain, uncuff the drain and call the GI team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep that right by my phone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you came in today with nausea and a low-grade fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I woke up feeling queasy, had chills, and my temperature was 99. I called my oncologist and he told me to come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good call. I see you have two biliary drains—one capped and one that usually drains into a bag. How much output do you normally get?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About 30 to 40 cc a day from the one on gravity. But today—nothing. I opened the other one too, just in case, and that’s dry as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s concerning. No output could mean a blockage. You also mentioned some right upper quadrant pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a little, especially when I cough. But it’s not sharp or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’ve checked your labs and your bilirubin is elevated. That, plus the fever and no drain output, makes us worry about a biliary obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like last time? But I just finished antibiotics a few weeks ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Given your history of cholangitis and E. coli bacteremia, we’ve started you on IV meropenem just in case. But we need to find out if the tube is blocked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get a chest X-ray to make sure there’s no infection in your lungs, and then tomorrow morning, interventional radiology will do a cholangiogram to look at the drain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And if it’s blocked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They may replace the tube. It’s a common procedure for patients like you. We’ll keep you on antibiotics until we know more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your liver enzymes are up—alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin are elevated. That supports the idea of a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not just in my head. I knew something was off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. The radiology team is reviewing your case now. You’re scheduled for a cholangiogram this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, the procedure is done. They found a blockage in the distal part of your PTBD tube. It was completely obstructed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So that’s why nothing was coming out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They removed the old tube and put in a new 8 French PTBD catheter. It’s now draining into a bag.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the same kind of tube I had before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same type but fresh. The old one likely got clogged with sludge or debris. This should fix the flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics? Do I still need them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re waiting on infectious disease to weigh in. Since your blood cultures are negative and you don’t have signs of active infection, they may stop them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Update: ID agrees. No signs of cholangitis—your fever’s gone, labs are stable. They don’t think you need more antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m off the IV meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll discontinue the meropenem. Your symptoms were likely from the blockage, not an active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about another round of sepsis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understandable. But you’re not showing signs of that now. Your drain is working, and your liver numbers should start to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your bilirubin dropped from 1.6 to 0.4 today. That’s a great sign the new tube is doing its job.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel better too—no nausea, no pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’re going to cap the drain later today to see if you tolerate it, just like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We capped the PTBD an hour ago. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine. No discomfort at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll keep it capped overnight. If you stay symptom-free, we can discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Home? That’d be nice. But what about the drain care?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Home health will visit you twice a week to check the site and manage the drain. You’ll also have a nurse teach you some basics before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You made it through the night with the drain capped—no issues. We’re clearing you to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Avoid heavy lifting. Keep the site clean and dry. Call us if you develop fever, pain, or the drain stops working again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my oncologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, follow up with him in a week. Your cancer is still being monitored, but no treatment changes now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my platelets? They’ve been low for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your platelet count is 81, which is low but stable for you. No intervention needed unless it drops further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’ll send all instructions with you, and home health will be at your house tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. I’ll keep an eye on things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You know your body best. Call us at the first sign of trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you came in with a fever and some changes in your drain output?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had a low fever yesterday—about 100.2. And I noticed green-yellow fluid coming from both drains. There’s also pus near the cholecystostomy site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any abdominal pain or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just some tenderness around the drain sites. No real belly pain. I’ve been a bit nauseous, but no vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of cholangiocarcinoma and past infections, we’re concerned this could be another biliary issue. We’ve started you on IV meropenem just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it another infection? I’ve had this before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. But your labs don’t show high white counts or liver enzyme spikes. We’re waiting on blood cultures. We’ll know more soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time it was a blocked drain. Could that be it again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we’re watching closely. If the drain is blocked, it can cause fluid buildup and look like infection. We may need to replace the tubes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds familiar. I hope it’s not serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do everything we can. For now, rest and let the antibiotics work while we monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative. No bacteria grew after 48 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not a bloodstream infection, at least. That makes us think the fever and discharge were due to a blockage or irritation, not active sepsis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So do I still need the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll stop the meropenem. Since you’re not febrile now and cultures are clean, continuing it isn’t necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But what about the green fluid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling a procedure tomorrow to check both drains. We’ll likely replace them to make sure they’re working properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get light sedation. Most patients tolerate it well. The team will walk you through it tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. Johnson. The procedure just finished. We replaced both the PTBD and the cholecystostomy tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How did it go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Well. The PTBD was blocked—contrast wouldn’t flow through. We cleared it with a balloon and put in a new catheter. The cholecystostomy tube was also exchanged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that was the problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The blockage likely caused the fluid backup and irritation. Now that it’s fixed, your symptoms should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I feel better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring your drain output and labs. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a CT scan yesterday as part of your oncology follow-up. The cholangiocarcinoma looks stable—no new lesions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Any change in the pancreas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s more dilation in the pancreatic duct, but it’s likely from the stents. Nothing suggests tumor growth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lungs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of spread. The small nodule is unchanged and not concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That lifts a weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Your platelets are stable too—65 on admission, now 78. No sign of worsening thrombocytopenia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No new triggers—no heparin, no recent chemo. It’s likely your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—we’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already? I feel fine, but is everything settled?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ve been afebrile for two days, labs are stable, and the drains are working. The issue was mechanical, not infectious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call or come back if you develop fever, abdominal pain, or if the drain output changes—like pus, blood, or stops altogether.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back to your usual—pantoprazole, atenolol, tamsulosin, dronabinol, and the others. No antibiotics needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the CT results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pending, but the radiologist says no progression. Your oncologist will review them fully at your next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the liver enzymes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wife will get instructions on drain care. Home health may check in too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She’s very helpful. I’m glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. We’ll see you in follow-up, but call sooner if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I restart the vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the drain site care?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve handled this well. Just take it easy for a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to. Rest sounds good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
